title: Rural and Urban Settings and Effective Learning Strategies
introduction: Human learning is shaped by the interaction between biological heredity and environmental settings—including family structure, rural or urban infrastructure, and classroom density[cite: 233, 235, 238, 239]. Beyond setting, individual differences in academic outcomes stem heavily from the learning strategies students adopt, making evidence-based study strategies essential for overcoming poor performance[cite: 241, 242].
learningOutcomes: 7.1 Define rural and urban settings demographically and explain how family variations and Bohannan's six types of divorce impact a child's learning and behaviour[cite: 232, 233].
7.2 Contrast Gesell's maturationist view with Watson's environmentalist view and differentiate phylogenic from ontogenetic functions[cite: 234, 235].

7.3 Analyze the educational challenges of rural and urban settings, including staffing, subject availability, ICT access, economic returns, cultural factors, and urban distractions[cite: 236, 237, 238].
7.4 Evaluate the four specific problems caused by classroom overcrowding on teaching and learning[cite: 238, 239, 240].

7.5 Explain and apply the seven paired effective learning strategies—spread vs. massed, recitation vs. reading, whole vs. part, knowledge of result, selective serial position, reinforcement, and motivation[cite: 242, 243, 244, 245, 246].

content.heading: Rural and Urban Settings, Family Variations, and Divorce
content.body: Rural and urban communities are typically distinguished using two demographic variables—absolute population size and settlement density—with most countries setting the rural-urban yardstick between 1,000 and 5,000 inhabitants[cite: 232]. Low population density and small community size in rural settings produce less frequent social contact per individual (reducing personal anonymity) and a restricted range of occupations and social roles (reducing heterogeneity compared to urban society)[cite: 232, 233]. Within both settings, traditional nuclear families now coexist with single-parent, stepparent, separated, divorced, non-marital, and communal family structures requiring ongoing adjustment[cite: 233]. Divorce increases family stress and often triggers acting out or disruptive behaviour at home and school; Bohannan (1970) identified six dimensions of divorce: emotional (deteriorating marriage), legal (formal grounds), economic (property division), co-parental (custody and visitation), community (altered friendships and social ties), and psychic (identity crisis and regaining autonomy)[cite: 233].

content.heading: Heredity, Maturation, and Environment Interaction
content.body: Observable traits such as hair colour, body build, height, weight, and partly intelligence depend on heredity, while environmental experience plays an increasing role as children grow[cite: 233]. Representing the heredity/maturation position, Arnold Gesell (founder of the Yale Clinic of Child Development, 1911; Gesell & Ilg, 1949; Gesell, 1954) defined maturation as genetically determined developmental potentials unfolding independently of training, setting limits that education can guide but not transcend and making proper timing (readiness) essential[cite: 234]. Conversely, the extreme environmentalist J. B. Watson (1926, 1928) rejected introspection and claimed that given a dozen healthy infants and a controlled environment, he could train any child at random into a doctor, lawyer, artist, or thief regardless of ancestry[cite: 234, 235]. Modern child psychologists recognize that heredity and environment interact[cite: 235]: phylogenic functions—such as crawling, creeping, sitting, and walking, along with sex, eye colour, and anatomical traits—have strong maturational bases resistant to early training or restriction (Dennis & Dennis, 1940; Smith, 1966)[cite: 235]. In contrast, ontogenetic functions—such as swimming, riding a bicycle, speaking English, or climbing a mountain—depend directly on environmental training, meaning culturally and educationally deprived settings prevent children from realizing their hereditary potential[cite: 235].

content.heading: Educational Challenges in Rural vs. Urban Settings
content.body: Rural and urban settings each present distinct advantages and learning obstacles[cite: 236, 238]. Rural schools struggle to attract and retain qualified specialty teachers (Grimmett & Echols, 2000), resulting in high turnover, heavy multi-subject workloads outside teachers' specialties, minimal mentoring, and difficulty building trust with students (Nielsen, 2004)[cite: 236]. Consequently, rural students have fewer opportunities to take senior science subjects required for post-secondary admission, face limited access to computers and Internet connectivity (ICT), and see lower economic returns on education because professional 'knowledge economy' jobs cluster in cities while rural unemployment is higher (Alasia, 2003; Looker, 2001; Alasia & Magnusson, 2005)[cite: 236, 237]. Lower rural family incomes also pull youths—especially males—out of school prematurely into the workforce, while out-migration of top rural students removes local educated role models[cite: 237]. Urban environments offer richer interpersonal interactions, libraries, museums, and mass media, whereas rural areas foster nature-oriented, farm-life, and traditional cultural learning (though pervasive rural superstitions can hinder scientific education)[cite: 238]. However, urban lifestyles introduce serious academic distractions, including night clubs, game centers, peer pressure, television/DSTV, cybercafés, and street hawking[cite: 238].

content.heading: Effects of Classroom Overcrowding on Learning
content.body: Classroom overcrowding—especially acute in urban Nigerian schools, where the average teacher-to-student ratio is roughly 1:45—strains public budgets, increases student disinterest, and lowers exam performance[cite: 238, 239]. Four specific problems arise from overcrowding[cite: 239]: (1) Students fail to receive individual attention because teachers spend class time managing seating and shared textbooks, leaving struggling readers behind[cite: 239]; (2) Teachers experience frustration, stress, and early burnout from heavy grading loads, strained facilities, constant discipline management, and inability to use innovative methods like cooperative group work[cite: 239]; (3) Students suffer low reading scores and lower achievement rates due to reduced attentiveness and long waits for teacher assistance[cite: 239]; and (4) Students struggle to concentrate or stay on task because of constant side attractions that a single teacher cannot fully supervise[cite: 239, 240].

content.heading: Effective Learning Strategies I: Spread, Recitation, and Whole Learning
content.body: Students who study hard with poor results sometimes blame witchcraft or juju spells, requiring Rational Emotive Therapy to replace superstition with evidence-based learning strategies[cite: 241, 242]. First, the Spread rather than Massed Learning Strategy respects brain fatigue limits: an adult brain works effectively for 50 to 60 minutes non-stop (and younger children for 30 to 40 minutes), after which 'reactive inhibition' lowers assimilation and causes 'brain-fag' (brain fatigue)[cite: 242, 320]. Spacing study with rest breaks therefore outperforms marathon non-stop reading[cite: 242]. Second, Recitation rather than Mere Reading activates all mental processes to recall material ('to cite again'); mental recitation outperforms verbal/vocal recitation and is practical in quiet public libraries, especially when paired with reading[cite: 242, 243]. Third, Whole rather than Part ('patristic') Learning applies the Gestalt principle that 'the whole is greater than the sum of its parts': learning a poem like 'Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star' or full words holistically preserves embedded meaning far better than isolating disconnected words or letters[cite: 243, 244].

content.heading: Effective Learning Strategies II: Feedback, Serial Position, Reinforcement, and Motivation
content.body: Fourth, Knowledge of Result (information feedback) rather than Non-Feedback prevents learners from operating 'blindfolded', helping them spot and fix errors or build on success[cite: 244]. Okoye (1981, 1987) emphasized delivering failure feedback tactfully so it does not erode self-concept, and choosing delayed feedback for creative tasks requiring mental fluidity while using immediate feedback for non-sensitive tasks[cite: 244]. Fifth, Selective Serial Position rather than Non-Selective Strategy leverages both the Primacy-Finality effect (first and last items in time or space are best learned) and the Von Restoff effect (unique middle items are also better learned—for example, the 1st, 4th, and 7th items in a seven-item series), guiding teachers to place key topics at the beginning, middle, or end of a lesson or term[cite: 245, 320, 323]. Sixth, Reinforcement rather than Non-Reinforcement pairs correct responses immediately with satisfiers (praise, recognition, rewards, promotions) to increase repetition, as shown in Skinner's box experiments[cite: 245, 246]. Seventh, Motivation rather than Non-Motivation avoids spoon-feeding and introduces moderate challenges that disrupt complacency/equilibrium, creating a psychological gap that rouses learners into purposeful action[cite: 246].

inTextQuestions.question: Distinguish between phylogenic functions and ontogenetic functions in child development.
inTextQuestions.answer: Phylogenic functions (such as crawling, creeping, sitting, and walking) have strong hereditary/maturational bases that emerge without formal training, whereas ontogenetic functions (such as swimming, riding a bicycle, or speaking English) require direct environmental training[cite: 235].

inTextQuestions.question: What is the optimal non-stop active learning span for adults versus younger children before reactive inhibition sets in?
inTextQuestions.answer: Adults can work effectively for 50 to 60 minutes non-stop, whereas younger children's effective span is 30 to 40 minutes before reactive inhibition reduces assimilation and leads to brain-fag[cite: 242, 320].

inTextQuestions.question: In a serial list of seven learning items, which three positions are predicted to be learned best according to the Primacy-Finality and Von Restoff effects?
When should a teacher use delayed knowledge of result rather than immediate knowledge of result?
inTextQuestions.answer: Delayed knowledge of result should be used for learning tasks involving creative skill and mental fluidity so the learner is not interrupted, whereas immediate feedback suits non-sensitive learning tasks[cite: 244].

saqs.question: Compare the positions of Arnold Gesell and J. B. Watson on heredity and environment, and explain how both factors interact in human learning.
saqs.answer: Gesell championed maturation (heredity), arguing that genetically determined potentials unfold with age and set limits that education can guide but not transcend[cite: 234]. Watson championed extreme environmentalism, claiming any healthy infant could be trained into any profession or character purely through environmental control[cite: 234, 235]. Both interact because heredity sets learning capacity and maturational readiness (governing phylogenic skills like walking), while the environment supplies essential training for ontogenetic skills (like reading or swimming) and shapes values, motivation, and realization of genetic potential[cite: 235, 236].

saqs.question: Discuss four educational challenges facing rural schools compared to urban schools, and name three urban lifestyle distractions that hinder learning.
saqs.answer: Four rural challenges are: (1) difficulty attracting and retaining qualified specialty teachers, causing high turnover and heavy multi-subject loads[cite: 236]; (2) fewer opportunities to study senior science subjects needed for post-secondary entry[cite: 236]; (3) poor access to computers and Internet (ICT)[cite: 236]; and (4) lower economic returns on education and low family incomes that push youths into early employment[cite: 237]. Three urban distractions are night clubs and game centers, television/DSTV or cybercafés, and hawking or negative peer influence[cite: 238].

saqs.question: Identify and explain the four specific problems caused by classroom overcrowding in schools.
saqs.answer: 1. Lack of individual attention: teachers spend class time managing seats and shared books, leaving weaker students behind[cite: 239]. 2. Teacher frustration and stress: heavy workloads, grading, discipline struggles, and scarce resources cause early burnout and block innovative group methods[cite: 239]. 3. Low reading scores: high student-to-teacher ratios lower attentiveness and delay help, reducing achievement[cite: 239]. 4. Poor concentration: numerous classroom side attractions prevent students from staying on task[cite: 239, 240].

saqs.question: Explain why spread learning, mental recitation, and whole learning are more effective than massed learning, mere reading, and part learning.
saqs.answer: Spread learning prevents reactive inhibition and brain-fag by inserting breaks after 50-60 minutes (adults) or 30-40 minutes (children)[cite: 242]. Mental recitation actively recruits all mental processes to recall material (outperforming passive reading and vocal recitation without disturbing library peers)[cite: 242, 243]. Whole learning aligns with Gestalt psychology by preserving overall context and meaning—such as learning a poem as a full verse—rather than fragmenting meaning through isolated part learning[cite: 243, 244].

saqs.question: Explain how a teacher can apply Knowledge of Result, Selective Serial Position, and Motivation strategies to improve classroom learning.
saqs.answer: Teachers should provide tactful Knowledge of Result so learners identify errors without damaging self-concept (immediate for routine tasks, delayed for creative fluidity)[cite: 244]; place the most critical curriculum topics at the start, middle, and end of lessons or terms to exploit Primacy-Finality and Von Restoff effects[cite: 245]; and avoid spoon-feeding by introducing moderate challenges that disrupt complacency and motivate active problem solving[cite: 246].
